Seven absorbing materials were tested at 160 GHz: FIRAM™-160, FIRAM™-500-red, FIRAM™-500-black, Rex Mat, AEL, neoprene wetsuit, and TK THz RAM.
Radar cross section (RCS) was measured at elevation angles from 15° to 75° and azimuth angles from 0° to 360°.
Wedged absorbers showed RCS peaks when wedges were perpendicular to incident radiation (at 90° and 270° azimuth).
Additional RCS peaks at 0° and 180° azimuth were caused by edge scattering from absorber edges.
FIRAM™-500-red had the lowest median HH RCS values (-51.2 dBsm at 15°, -39.6 dBsm at 75°).
FIRAM™-500-red had high transmittance (-9.6 dB parallel, -9.0 dB perpendicular), complicating RCS comparisons.
Neoprene wetsuit had relatively high RCS despite high transmittance (-10.7 dB), attributed to volumetric scattering.
TK THz RAM showed multiple periodic RCS peaks with spacing increasing from ~15° at 15° elevation to ~90° at 75° elevation.
FIRAM™-160 and TK THz RAM had similar median HH RCS values around -40 to -35 dBsm and low transmittance (-61.0 dB and -41.7 dB respectively).
RCS generally increased with elevation angle for all materials tested.
HH (horizontal transmit/horizontal receive) and VV (vertical receive) polarizations showed similar RCS behavior.
ISAR imagery revealed spatial scattering features and confirmed edge scattering contributions.
The compact radar range used a low-RCS aluminum pylon tilted 10° forward to minimize backscatter.
Materials were approximately 24 in. x 24 in. in size; TK THz RAM was assembled from 36 tiles of 4 in. x 4 in.
Measurements were limited to a narrow frequency band centered at 160 GHz and a limited angular range.
The study aimed to understand general backscattering behavior rather than rank absorber performance.
Edge scattering would be reduced in practical applications by joining absorbers into large panels.
The neoprene wetsuit was a poor candidate for high-performance THz absorption due to scattering.
The pyramidal TK THz RAM's scattering features diminished at higher elevation angles, near its intended use angle.
The study was supported by the U.S. Army National Ground Intelligence Center.
